scope: Agent read actual authored speech segments and callout copy from all10 pinned original-producer plans and compared them with primary mechanism descriptions for their selected constructions. This establishes input-copy/source consistency only, not physical assembly correctness, actual spoken performance, final encoded label/leader truth, full factual review, portability or human acceptance. No product QA seals are changed or transferred to a new runtime.

rows.question: Why does the hook on a tape measure move?

source.observedTitle: Why does the hook on the end of the Stanley tape rule move?
source.locator: Explanatory paragraphs on travel, outside and inside measurement.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: Why does this tape-measure hook slide?
Wouldn’t that mess up the measurement?
Hook it over an edge, and you’re
measuring from its INSIDE face.
Push it against a wall, and you
use its OUTSIDE face.
Those faces are a thickness of metal
apart.
So the hook slides by that SAME
distance.
That tiny movement keeps the hook’s own
thickness out of your measurement.

supportedClaims: Hook travel compensates for its thickness.
Pulling an edge and pushing a wall select opposite contact faces.
The copy describes the thickness offset rather than claiming a measured manufacturing tolerance.
explicitInferences: Face names follow the declared selected hook construction; actual rendered leader destinations still need inspection.
rows.limits: Floating-hook tape rule; no universal claim for every end fitting or quantitative accuracy certification.

rows.question: Why does a cable tie tighten but resist pulling backward?
rows.selectedDesign: one-piece outside-serrated nylon cable tie with integral rooted plastic tongue

source.locator: FAQ: How does a cable tie fastener work? and Cable ties with plastic pawls.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: A zip tie slides tighter.
So why won’t it slide BACK?
Inside the head, each passing tooth bends
a little plastic tongue out of the
way.
The tongue springs into the next gap,
ready for another tooth.
But reverse direction, and a tooth catches
against that tongue.
The same contact that lets the tie
tighten stops it opening back up.

supportedClaims: A flexible tongue engages strap serrations and resists reverse withdrawal.
For the described one-piece tie the tongue is integral with the head.
The passing-tooth and return explanation is consistent with this flexible positive-locking construction.
explicitInferences: Elastic return into successive serrations is an inference from the flexible integral pawl; no force or fatigue calculation is claimed.
rows.limits: Selected outside-serrated plastic-pawl tie; exclude toothless KR pins, steel balls and releasable variants.

rows.question: Why does squeezing one end of a clothespeg open the other?
rows.selectedDesign: Conventional wooden two-arm peg around US4063333A Fig7; reconstructed seated normal state, excluding improved retention parts

source.locator: Saved primary HTML: conventional clothespin61/members64,65/spring66; FIG.7 description and spring seating paragraphs.
source.webLimit: Direct /en and locale-free opens returned Internal Error. Search retrieved the improved invention abstract; the conventional mechanism was actually read in the saved primary HTML, not inferred from that search abstract.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: Let go of this clothespeg.
It’s STILL squeezing.
Squeeze the handles, and the wooden arms
rock around their middle, opening the jaws
and loading the metal spring.
Release them, and the spring closes the
jaws again.
But the fabric keeps them slightly apart,
so the spring stays loaded.
Your HAND has stopped squeezing.
The SPRING hasn’t.

supportedClaims: Manually pressing the rear portions overcomes the spring and opens the gripping jaws.
The conventional construction has a metal coiled spring seated between the two arms with ends retained in outer recesses.
The script consistently distinguishes continued spring grip from the removed hand force.
explicitInferences: Residual spring load while fabric holds the jaws apart is an elastic-mechanism inference, not a calibrated holding-force result.
rows.limits: Conventional spring peg only. FIG.7 is explicitly an unstable failure pose; do not copy it as the operating pose or adopt the improved clips/pin construction.

rows.question: How does a zipper join its teeth?
rows.selectedDesign: US1219881A metal-element zipper: identical staggered projection/recess members with a diverging-channel slider; YKK general tunnel explanation as corroboration.

source.locator: Description of locking projection10/recess11, slider6/tongue, Y-shaped channels; claims on direction-dependent joining/separation.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: One zipper slider.
Two opposite jobs.
Pull it one way, and the
teeth join.
Pull it back, and they separate.
Inside is a Y-shaped channel.
It guides the two rows together,
lining up matching bumps and hollows
so the metal teeth interlock.
Reverse the slider, and its divider
guides those teeth apart into the
two branches.
Same channel, opposite journey.

supportedClaims: Metal elements interlock through corresponding projections and recesses.
The slider guides the two rows together in one direction and separates them in the other.
The divider and branching channel explanation matches the selected metal-element construction.
rows.limits: Metal cup-element zipper, not every coil/molded or reverse-coil design; no inter-element collision freedom established.

rows.question: How does a keyhole mounting slot hold a screw?
rows.selectedDesign: Conventional keyhole slot disclosed in EP1817988A1 background: enlarged entry then narrower shank track, without the invention’s additional snap neck.

source.locator: Description of head19/shank18, larger portion22/narrow portion23; separate neck24 snap-fit discussion.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: This hole lets a screw head through.
Then a short slide traps it.
The head enters through the wide opening.
Slide the plate, and the screw’s thinner
shaft moves into the narrow slot.
Now the wider head overlaps the edges.
Pull straight outward?
The head blocks the plate.
Slide it BACK to the wide opening,
and the head can pass through again.

supportedClaims: The larger opening admits the head; the narrower section can admit the shank while excluding that head.
Transverse movement positions the shank within the narrow section and head overlap prevents direct axial pull-through.
The script does not promise resistance to sliding back toward the entry.
explicitInferences: Simple reverse release follows from the selected plain, unlatched slot geometry. The cited patent also describes a restrictive snap-fit neck that is explicitly excluded here.
rows.limits: Plain keyhole-slot principle only; exclude the patent neck/snap-fit, washers or detents and unverified load/security ratings.

rows.question: Why do binder-clip handles make the jaws open?
rows.selectedDesign: US1139627A continuous triangular sheet-steel binder, integral rolled jaw journals and body-bearing wire levers; authored U-handle proportions, clamping action only

source.locator: Description of resilient sheet-metal body, spring-steel sidesA/B and back; operating handles/leversD and fulcrum.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: Where’s the spring in this binder clip?
You’re looking at it.
The folded steel BODY.
Squeeze the wire handles, and they act
as levers, bending that body open.
Let go, and the steel pushes back
toward its original shape.
Paper keeps the jaws apart and the
body slightly bent, so it keeps pressing.
The handles give you leverage.
The BODY supplies the grip.

supportedClaims: The folded spring-steel body supplies resilient jaw force.
The wire handles operate as levers against the body to spread the gripping edges.
The copy attributes leverage to the handles and grip to the body rather than inventing a separate coil spring.
explicitInferences: Continued pressure when paper holds the body away from its unloaded form is an elastic-mechanism inference; no force or material-grade measurement.
rows.limits: Selected conventional spring-steel binder clip; do not infer every clip has identical bearings, force or steel specification.

rows.question: How does a side-release buckle lock and release?
rows.selectedDesign: US5546642A improved side-release buckle embodiment with resilient male arms, upper/lower abutments and female release actuators.

source.locator: Arms24/abutments38,40; retaining surfaces60; side actuators66; coupling/uncoupling description.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: Pull this buckle, and it holds.
Squeeze the sides, and it opens.
What changed?
In this version, two flexible arms bend
inward as the halves join.
Then their raised edges spring outward behind
stops inside the housing.
Pulling presses those edges against the stops.
Squeeze BOTH side buttons, and the arms
bend inward again.
Their edges clear the stops.
Now the halves can separate.

supportedClaims: Insertion flexes the male arms until retaining and abutment surfaces engage.
Withdrawal loads those retaining contacts.
Side actuators move the arms inward until the abutments clear and the halves can separate.
rows.limits: The script explicitly limits this to the selected version with female side actuators; exclude a universal claim about all side-release buckles.

rows.question: Why does a door latch retract and spring back?
rows.selectedDesign: US10837199B2 latch550 closing subassembly, Figs16–18: cam face556, spring570 and fixed boss572; show the closing stroke rather than the separate deadlocking system.

source.observedTitle: US10837199B2 — Cylindrical latch bolt assembly having beveled blocking surface
source.locator: FIGS.16A/16B: inclined closing cam556; bolt550; bolt spring570 and fixed boss572.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: You push this door shut without turning
the handle.
So what moves the latch?
Its sloping face hits the metal plate
on the frame.
That contact pushes the bolt back into
the door, compressing its spring.
Then the bolt reaches the plate’s opening.
There’s room to move OUT again.
The spring pushes the bolt into that
opening, catching the door shut.

supportedClaims: The inclined closing cam contacts the strike while the door closes and retracts the bolt.
The bolt spring reacts against a fixed boss and biases the bolt outward.
Extension into the strike opening provides the described catch.
explicitInferences: Spring compression/release while the strike constrains and then clears the bolt follows from that documented arrangement.
rows.limits: Ordinary closing-cam explanation only; distinguish it from the patent blocking surface560 and deadlatch trigger/security features. No locking/security certification.

rows.question: Why is a tape-measure blade curved?
rows.selectedDesign: Conventional transverse curved blade in WO2020159114A1 background Fig.2; explicit flattening comparison and authored exposed teaching mandrel

source.locator: Translated background, conventional blade1/FIG.2: transverse curved profile, self-weight bending and flattening onto bobbin3.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: This tape-measure blade changes shape to do
two jobs.
Look ACROSS its width.
That shallow curve helps the strip resist
drooping along its length.
But watch what happens as it winds
onto the reel.
The side-to-side curve flattens, letting the blade
bend around the spool.
Curved across its width for support.
Flattened across its width so it can
roll up.

supportedClaims: Transverse curvature helps the extended blade resist lengthwise droop.
That transverse profile flattens as the blade is wound onto its bobbin.
The script remains qualitative and gives no stiffness ratio or standout-length claim.
rows.limits: Conventional curved blade described in the background; exclude the proposed grooves/multiple-curvature improvements. English source is a Korean machine translation.

rows.question: How does a soda-can tab open the scored panel?
rows.selectedDesign: US6575684B2 first stay-on lid embodiment: tab42/44, rivet16, bendable flange46, tongue17 and score58 ending in hinge19.

source.locator: Flange46/rivet16 and forward bending region; tab heel44/nose42; score18 head60/tail62 and retained hinge19; opening description.

spokenSegmentsRead.text: Lift this can tab, and its nose
pushes DOWN.
In this design, the rivet holds a
thin metal attachment.
That attachment bends as the tab tilts,
letting the nose press the panel below.
The panel opens along a weakened line.
But look—the line stops short.
That remaining strip acts as a hinge,
keeping the panel attached as it folds
inward.

supportedClaims: The rivet clamps the tab flange while a nearby flange portion can bend as the tab tilts.
Lifting the heel drives the nose against the panel and opens the score.
Material between the score ends remains a bending hinge retaining the opening tongue.
rows.limits: The script explicitly limits this to the selected retained-flange stay-on-tab design. Do not describe the rivet as a free pin hinge or infer all can ends use identical geometry.
